column4: The section explicitly cites this wording as a secondary sense of ānastum (آنَسْتُم): guardians should see sound judgment in the orphans before returning property. It extends “noticing a fire” to recognizing maturity.
When lightning illuminates the people, they walk by its light; when darkness returns, they stop. This closely parallels the section’s night traveler moving toward a visible fire.
This preceding ayah sets the thunderstorm, darkness, and lightning; 2:20 adds the people walking when its light appears, completing the wayfinding scene.
The ayah makes night and day signs, effaces the night sign, and makes the day sign visible; it gives another specific account of light and darkness as alternating signs.
The fire’s enclosure surrounds the wrongdoers (أَحَاطَ بِهِمْ سُرَادِقُهَا), a direct parallel to the sealed fire over people in the section.
This ayah says God made roads in the earth so people may be guided, another explicit road-and-guidance formulation alongside the section’s beacon and the roadways in 16:15 and 43:10.
The ayah depicts layered darkness in the deep sea, with no light for the person God has left without light; it is a specific absence-of-illumination counterpart to the fire named for light.
The Messenger is called an illuminating lamp (سِرَاجًا مُّنِيرًا) and a caller to God; this joins light to guidance as the section does with a road beacon.
Night is stripped from day and people are left in darkness; this makes the section’s hidden night and its seen fire into a concrete day-to-night transition.
This ayah says God made fire from the green tree and people kindle it, another direct account of the fire whose root the section connects to illumination.
Saqar neither leaves nor spares anything; this gives the punitive fire an unrelenting force that reverses the section’s useful, resting fire.
The next ayah says the fire scorches human skin; it specifies the bodily effect of the Saqar described in 74:28.
The shade offered in the fire scene gives no shade and cannot protect from the flame, reversing the section’s fire as a waymark and a place to rest by.
The next ayah describes sparks cast from the flame like palaces; it continues the fire scene with a visible, outward-moving image.
This ayah says the orphan is not honored; it opens a passage that contrasts with the section’s uphill acts of care before its final fire.
This ayah says people do not urge one another to feed the poor, a direct reversal of the section’s feeding and mercy before the companions of the Fire are named.
The passage adds devouring inheritance greedily; it continues the contrast between the section’s care for the needy and the conduct associated with the later Fire.
This ayah names excessive love of wealth, directly matching the section’s hoarder and the boast about amassed wealth in its surah.

Here Hell is brought forth. Earlier in this surah, 89:17–20 names neglect of orphans and the poor and excessive love of wealth, dispositions that echo the section’s contrast between care and the sealed fire.
The next ayah says no one punishes as God punishes on that day; it intensifies the judgment scene begun when Hell is brought forth in 89:23.
The following ayah says none binds as God binds; this adds a specific confinement image to the Hell scene introduced in 89:23.
The section’s source list includes raʾā (رءي) in the claim that a person thinks no one sees him; this ayah asks whether he knows that God sees, directly answering that presumption.
The next ayah has Abraham see the moon and note that it sets; this plausibly extends the section’s night scene of a traveler seeing a light, though the moon here is not offered as a guide.
The following ayah has Abraham see the sun and note that it sets; this plausibly extends the section’s seen-light scene, while its argument about created lights is not explicit in the fire passage.
Abraham turns toward the Creator of the heavens and earth after the star, moon, and sun set; this continues 6:76–78 and complements the section’s question about who makes the fire.
The hypocrites avoid the heat of the expedition, but are told Hell’s fire is hotter; it reverses worldly avoidance of heat against the surah’s difficult path and the section’s final fire.
